## DP3 in the SKA Science Data Processor

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- DP3: LOFAR pipeline software (ASTRON): averaging, flagging, calibration, prediction
- Used for the preprocessing / self-calibration engine of the SKA Science Data Processor
- Self-calibration alternates **predict** (simulate a model sky) and **solve** (fit corrections against it)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{python}
#| fig-height: 2
_ = plotting.predict_share()
```
:::
:::

## The predict step

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Simulates model visibilities for every baseline × channel × correlation, from a sky model and a telescope model
- Per source: simulate its contribution, accumulate into a per-patch buffer
- Per patch: compute the beam response, apply it to that patch's buffer
- Mostly DP3 internal implementation; calls EveryBeam for the beam response
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
plotting.reference_workload_table()
```
:::
:::

## Original work distribution

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
**Structure:**

- Sources statically split into equal-count slices, one per thread
- Each thread simulates its sources and computes beam responses independently into a private accumulator

**Potential issues:**

- Can result in a workload discrepancy
- Beam computations are duplicated when shared among multiple threads
:::
::: {.column width="40%" .nowrap}
```{python}
plotting.baseline_headline_table()
```
:::
:::

## Per-thread load

```{python}
#| fig-height: 3.5
_ = plotting.per_thread_load()
imb = plotting.baseline_imbalance_split()
mix = plotting.component_mix()
```

- Flat item count: `{python} f"{imb['items_lo']}–{imb['items_hi']}"` sources on
  every thread, yet thread time spreads
  **`{python} f"{imb['range_spread']:.1f}x"`**
- `simulate()` itself only spreads
  `{python} f"{imb['simulate_spread']:.1f}x"` —
  `{python} f"{mix['gaussian_pct']:.0f}%"` of components are Gaussian, so an
  equal-count split gives every thread much the same mix
- The spread is in the rest: the beam-apply remainder varies
  **`{python} f"{imb['other_spread']:.1f}x"`** across threads and is
  `{python} f"{imb['other_share_pct']:.0f}%"` of thread busy time
- Equal *source* counts are not equal *patch* counts — and the beam fires per patch

## Dynamic dispatch via Intel Thread Building Blocks (TBB) library

```{python}
#| fig-height: 4
plotting.work_stealing_diagram()
```

- Same per-source granularity as the static split, dispatched dynamically through `tbb::parallel_for` instead of a fixed slice per thread
- Work-stealing scheduler: idle threads pick up remaining sources instead of sitting still
- Low overhead scheduler + minimal code to maintain

- Better per-thread time balance
- Only `{python} f"{work['makespan_gain_pct']:.0f}%"` of total time saved:
  total work grew
  `{python} f"{work['work_growth_pct']:.0f}%"`
  (`{python} f"{work['static_total_s']:.0f}"` → `{python} f"{work['tbb_total_s']:.0f}"` thread-seconds)
- Because of too many beam application calls that could be mutualized!

## Removing the redundant beam applies

```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.5
acc = plotting.patch_accumulator_cost()
plotting.dispatch_variants_diagram()
```

- Structural redundancy: a patch's beam apply fires once per patch
  **per range**, so the finer the stealing, the more applies
- Tried several variants:
    - Patch parallelism: too coarse, compute time still heterogeneous
    - Thread-local/patch-local accumulators: high memory consumption and high pressure on memory bandwidth
    - Pipeline based approach with task stealing and queues: complex and low performance benefit

    ==> General conclusion: tradeoff between parallelism efficiency and memory overhead

## Tile by channel and source

```{python}
#| fig-height: 4.5
plotting.tiling_diagram()
```

- Each thread works a channel slab × source block tile sized to stay inside
  L2, instead of every source sweeping the full channel range
- Current implementation only works on unpolarized sky models
- **Hypothesis**: expected to cut cache misses and reduce pressure on DDR

## Impact of the new layout

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{python}
#| fig-height: 3.5
layout = plotting.progression_bars("tiled_layout")
```
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
- `{python} f"{plotting.fmt_int_html(layout['before'])}s → {plotting.fmt_int_html(layout['after'])}s"` predict time,
  **`{python} f"{layout['speedup']:.2f}x"`**
- Beam applications are done on-the-fly in the in the Stokes-I path
  so the per-patch buffer round-trip disappears
  `{python} f"{work['static_beam_s']:.0f}"`s of thread time to
  `{python} f"{work['tiled_beam_s']:.1f}"`s
:::
:::

## Vectorizing the inner loops {.smaller}

```{python}
loops = plotting.loop_progression()
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| fig-height: 4.6
plotting.inner_loop_diagram()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.7
plotting.loop_progression_bars()
```

- Structure of arrays pattern for processing, then written into array of structures
- Slab rounded to a multiple of an SIMD lane to avoid scalar epilogues
- `xsimd::sincos` in `phases()` and `xsimd::exp` in the Gaussian envelope
- Combined performance gain:
  `{python} f"{loops['before']:.2f}s → {loops['after']:.2f}s"` per normal
  timestep, **`{python} f"{loops['speedup']:.1f}x"`**
  (`{python} f"{loops['total_speedup']:.2f}x"` on the whole predict step)
:::
:::

## Conclusion / discussion

- Correctness: unit tests + results validated on a realistic test case
- Good performance gains through a loop reordering
- Takeaway:
  - a better scheduler alone had a ceiling close to the baseline
  - it balanced the threads much better
  - but paid for it in both compute and memory accesses from redundant per-patch work
  - the real gain came from reordering memory access
- Perspective:
    - polarized sky models. The tiled path needs Stokes I today; applying the Jones matrix per patch **per channel slab** keeps the tile in L2 and saves memory traffic
    - GPU implementation
    - applying FastPredict improvements (look into trigonometry lookup tables, source type batching, some possible precompute)
